passages.t: ‘How lovely are your tents, O Jacob’
passages.happening:
This time Balaam does not go aside to look for omens. “When Balaam looked up and saw Israel encamped tribe by tribe, the Spirit of God came upon him” (verse 2).

He speaks his third oracle. “How lovely are your tents, O Jacob, your dwellings, O Israel!” (verse 5). They spread out ‘like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream’ (verse 6). Water will flow from Israel's buckets. Its king will be great and its kingdom lifted high (verse 7). God brought this people out of Egypt (verse 8).

“He crouches, he lies down like a lion; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him? Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Something changes at the start of this chapter. On the first two hills Balaam went off alone to seek signs, as a seer of his world would. Verse 1 says he now gave that up. The Hebrew word means the reading of omens. He simply turns, looks at the camp, and the Spirit of God comes on him.

What he sees is the camp of chapter 2: the tribes in their places around the tabernacle. Thirty-eight years of wandering lie behind those tents. A whole generation has been buried. And the order God gave at Sinai is still there. Seen from above by an outsider, it is beautiful.

The oracle's opening calls Balaam ‘a man whose eyes are open’. That has a point after the donkey. The seer who could not see an angel in the road now truly sees.

The pictures in verses 5 to 7 belong to a dry land. Palm groves, gardens by a stream, cedars beside water, buckets running over: to people who had lived forty years in the desert these were pictures of a settled and plentiful life.

The oracle ends by quoting Genesis, though Balaam may not have known it. The crouching lion is from Jacob's blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:9). The last line is God's first promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3). A foreign seer, hired to undo Israel, ends up reciting the promises on which Israel stands.

‘Greater than Agag’ in verse 7 looks ahead. Agag was a king of the Amalekites whom Israel's first king, Saul, fought centuries later (1 Samuel 15). Readers who date the oracles late think the line was written with that history in view. Readers who accept their early setting take it as true prediction. These notes do not settle it.
passages.later:
Jacob had said of his son Judah, “Like a lion he crouches and lies down; like a lioness, who dares to rouse him?” (Genesis 49:9).

God had said to Abraham, “I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). The promise was never for Israel alone. It was for the good of every family on earth.
passages.asks: Balaam looked at a people who had failed for forty years and saw something lovely, because he saw them as God had ordered them. Ask how you look at your own church or family: by the list of their failures, or by what God has made of them. And ask whose good you could speak of today, in their hearing or out of it.

passages.happening:
Balak is furious. He strikes his hands together and tells Balaam to go home without his pay (verses 10-11). Balaam reminds him of what he said at the start: not for a house full of silver and gold could he go beyond the LORD's command (verse 13). Then, unasked, he offers one more word, about ‘what this people will do to your people in the days to come’ (verse 14).

“I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near. A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel. He will crush the skulls of Moab and strike down all the sons of Sheth” (verse 17).

Edom will become a possession. “A ruler will come from Jacob” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The fourth oracle is different from the others. No one paid for it and no altars were built. Balaam gives it freely, and it reaches far beyond the day on which it was spoken.

‘I see him, but not now.’ The opening lines say that the subject lies in the distant future. Balaam sees a single figure, ‘him’, and names him with two pictures. A star: in the ancient Near East kings were often compared to stars. A scepter: the staff that marked a ruler. The Hebrew word for scepter here is the one in Jacob's promise that the scepter would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10). The oracle takes that promise further. A king will rise in Israel.

He is described as a king of his world would be described, by his victories over the neighboring peoples. The language is the hard language of ancient royal poetry. The first to match the description was David, who some centuries later brought Moab and Edom under his rule (2 Samuel 8:2, 14). The phrase ‘sons of Sheth’ is obscure. It may name a people of the region, but no one is sure.

These lines are no reason for contempt toward Moabites or Edomites or anyone descended from them. The Bible itself guards against that reading. David, the king who first fits this oracle, was the great-grandson of a Moabite woman, Ruth (Ruth 4:13-17). Matthew names her among the ancestors of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

The oracle did not stop with David. Long after his kingdom had fallen, Jews went on reading it as a promise of a king still to come.
passages.later:
The scepter was first promised to Judah: “The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet” (Genesis 49:10).

Matthew tells of wise men from the east who came to Jerusalem asking, “Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews? We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him” (Matthew 2:2). Matthew does not quote Balaam. Many readers have heard an echo, since the Magi, like Balaam, are foreigners from the east who see what Israel's own rulers miss.

In the last chapter of the Bible Jesus says, “I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star” (Revelation 22:16).
passages.hard:
Who is the star? How have Jewish and Christian readers understood this verse?

Both begin from the same place. The oracle speaks of a king who will arise in Israel in days far off from Balaam's own.

In Israel's history the words first came true in David. He defeated Moab and Edom, as verses 17 and 18 describe. Scholars who date the oracles late think they were written with David in view. Those who accept their early setting read them as prediction. On either view David is the first figure the words fit.

Jewish readers in the centuries before Jesus read further. David's kingdom had ended, and they understood the star as a ruler still to come, an anointed king, which is the meaning of the word messiah. The Dead Sea Scrolls quote the verse in that sense. In AD 132 Simon bar Kosiba led the second Jewish revolt against Rome, and he was hailed as Bar Kokhba, which means son of the star, in a clear reference to this verse. The revolt ended in defeat in 135. The hope for the king the verse promises did not end with it, and that reading belongs to Jewish faith in its own right. Christians should describe it with respect.

Christians inherited the same messianic reading from Judaism and hold that the king has come in Jesus. They do not usually claim that Balaam described how he would come. Matthew's story of the star does not quote the verse. The New Testament calls Jesus the son of David and the Morning Star (Revelation 22:16), and it tells of a star at his birth (Matthew 2:2). Christians read David's kingdom as a pattern of a greater reign. They also hold that this king does not conquer as verse 17 pictures David conquering. He said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36), and those who belong to it are told to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44).

So Jews and Christians agree that the verse promises a king from Israel, and that David alone does not exhaust it. They differ on whether that king has come. These notes are written from Christian faith, and they can state the difference honestly without belittling those who read the verse otherwise.

No one may take the warlike words of verse 17 as a pattern or a warrant for violence against any people.
passages.asks: Balaam saw the king from a great distance and went home unchanged. Ask whether you know true things about Christ that have made no difference to how you live. And ask what it means to you that the one promised here came for the good of all the families of the earth, the families of his people's old enemies included.

passages.t: Last words, and the two men part
passages.happening:
Balaam looks out and speaks short sayings about other peoples. Of Amalek: ‘first among the nations, but his end is destruction’ (verse 20). Of the Kenites: their home is secure, like a nest in a cliff, yet Asshur will carry them away (verses 21-22). And at the last: “Ah, who can live unless God has ordained it?” (verse 23). Ships will come from the coasts of Cyprus, and those powers too will pass (verse 24).

“Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The story ends quietly. After three hills, twenty-one altars and four oracles, the two men simply go home. Balak has spent a great deal and gained nothing. Not one word against Israel has been spoken.

The short sayings look out at the peoples round about. Amalek was a people of the southern desert who had attacked Israel soon after the exodus (Exodus 17:8-13). The Kenites were a clan linked with Moses' family by marriage, who lived among or near Israel (Judges 1:16). Asshur is Assyria, the empire that would rule the region centuries later. The ‘coasts of Cyprus’ translate the Hebrew Kittim, a name first used for Cyprus and later for peoples from across the sea to the west.

The sayings are hard in places, and scholars differ over the details. Their drift is clear. One power after another rises and falls. Empires that seem permanent are not. Verse 23 says it in a line: no one lives unless God has ordained it.

And Balaam? He goes home having spoken some of the truest words in the book. They did him no good. Chapter 31 will say that the plot which led Israel into sin at Peor came from his advice (31:16), and that he died by the sword among Israel's enemies (31:8). The hard question below asks how such a man could speak for God.
passages.later:
Daniel, living under a later empire, said the same as verse 23 in his own words: God ‘removes kings and establishes them’ (Daniel 2:21).

The risen Jesus warns a church about people who ‘hold to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites’ (Revelation 2:14). The warning is addressed to Christians.
passages.hard:
How could a foreign seer, who later did Israel great harm, speak true prophecy?

The Bible is plain that Balaam was not a faithful servant of God. This book blames his advice for the sin at Peor (31:16). The New Testament remembers him for greed and for teaching others to stumble (2 Peter 2:15; Revelation 2:14). Yet in this chapter the Spirit of God comes on him, and he speaks words the rest of Scripture treats as true.

Readers have answered that the truth of a prophecy rests in God who gives it, and not in the one who speaks it. God made a donkey speak two chapters ago. John's Gospel says that the high priest Caiaphas, who was plotting the death of Jesus, ‘was prophesying that Jesus would die for the nation’ without knowing what he said (John 11:51).

The story also holds a warning. Balaam had words from God, and even a sight of the far future, and his heart was not changed by them. Jesus said that on the last day some will say, “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name”, and will hear that he never knew them (Matthew 7:22-23). A gift is not the same thing as faithfulness.

That warning is meant for people who use spiritual gifts and words while serving themselves. It is not aimed at the anxious believer who fears that their own faith may be false.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Balaam spoke the truth about God and went home the same man. Ask whether there is a truth you can explain well and have never obeyed. And ask what empire, institution or security of your own day you treat as permanent, when verse 23 says that nothing stands unless God ordains it.
